records.text: Recurrent neural networks suffer from vanishing gradients.
In recurrent neural networks, the same weight matrix W is multiplied at every time step.
If the spectral radius of W is less than 1, gradients decay to zero.
Exploding gradients cause obvious numerical overflows.
Vanishing gradients are silent.
With vanishing gradients, the loss may still decrease because W trains on the last few steps.
With vanishing gradients, the network loses long-term memory.
With vanishing gradients, the network can no longer base predictions on early parts of a sequence.
A solution to vanishing gradients is to create a constant error carousel.
The constant error carousel is a highway where the gradient can flow unchanged without being repeatedly multiplied by weight matrices.
The constant error carousel was inspired by ResNet-style residual connections.
The constant error carousel insight was pioneered in Jürgen Schmidhuber’s group in the mid-1990s.
The LSTM was introduced in Hochreiter & Schmidhuber (1995) and Gers & Schmidhuber (2000).
The LSTM cell maintains a cell state c_t.
The cell state c_t lives on the gradient highway.
The LSTM cell maintains a hidden state h_t.
The hidden state h_t participates in the cell's operations.
Information flow in the LSTM is controlled by three gates: input, forget, and output.
Each gate is a small sub-network.
Each gate outputs a vector of values in (0,1) via the logistic sigmoid.
Each gate multiplies other vectors component-wise to erase, write, or read from memory.
The LSTM has a clear, interpretable program that allows deleting selected parts of memory, adding new values, and deciding what to expose to the output.
The candidate cell state c'_t is computed as c'_t = tanh(W_{xc} x_t + W_{hc} h_{t-1} + b_{c'}).
The input gate i_t is computed as i_t = σ(W_{xi} x_t + W_{hi} h_{t-1} + b_i).
The forget gate f_t is computed as f_t = σ(W_{xf} x_t + W_{hf} h_{t-1} + b_f).
The output gate o_t is computed as o_t = σ(W_{xo} x_t + W_{ho} h_{t-1} + b_o).
The cell state update is c_t = f_t ⊙ c_{t-1} + i_t ⊙ c'_t.
The block output is h_t = o_t ⊙ tanh(c_t).
If the forget gate f_t is fully open (f_t = 1), c_t = c_{t-1} + i_t ⊙ c'_t.
If f_t = 1, then the partial derivative ∂c_t/∂c_{t-1} = 1.
This allows gradients to flow unchanged, i.e., the constant error carousel property.
In the basic LSTM, the gates only see the hidden state h_{t-1} = o_{t-1} ⊙ tanh(c_{t-1}).
If the output gate is closed in the LSTM, the LSTM's behaviour becomes independent of the cell state.
Peephole connections give the gates direct access to c_{t-1}.
Peephole connections add extra weight matrices W_{pi}, W_{pf}, W_{po} to the gate equations.
The input gate with peephole is computed as i_t = σ(W_{xi} x_t + W_{hi} h_{t-1} + W_{pi} c_{t-1} + b_i).
The forget gate with peephole is computed as f_t = σ(W_{xf} x_t + W_{hf} h_{t-1} + W_{pf} c_{t-1} + b_f).
The output gate with peephole is computed as o_t = σ(W_{xo} x_t + W_{ho} h_{t-1} + W_{po} c_{t-1} + b_o).
The basic LSTM uses 8 weight matrices.
The basic LSTM weight matrices consist of four pairs of size d×d and d×d'.
d is typically 256–1000.
Peephole connections add three more weight matrices.
The LSTM is memory-heavy.
The LSTM is extremely effective.
The LSTM has remained the most important recurrent cell since its final form in 2000.
LSTMs are the standard in recent large-scale systems such as AlphaStar.
As of the lecture date, no alternative recurrent cell consistently outperforms the LSTM in general.
A classic toy task from Hochreiter and Schmidhuber demonstrates why gated cells are necessary.
The input has two channels: one fills a stream of random numbers, the other contains zeros except for exactly two "marker" ones.
The goal is to output the sum of the two random numbers that coincided with the markers.
A plain RNN fails completely on this task because it cannot store the first marked number long enough to add it to the second.
An LSTM learns to open its write gate exactly on the markers, store the relevant number in the cell state, and later recall it.
The running prediction of the LSTM tracks the true sum perfectly.
Gated cells are the only way to achieve this kind of long-range memory.
Many attempts have been made to simplify the LSTM while keeping the constant error carousel.
Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) were introduced by Cho et al. (2014).
GRU merges the cell state and hidden state into a single vector h_t.
GRU uses only two gates: update gate u_t and reset gate r_t.
The update gate in GRU is computed as u_t = σ(W_{xu} x_t + W_{hu} h_{t-1} + b_u).
The reset gate in GRU is computed as r_t = σ(W_{xr} x_t + W_{hr} h_{t-1} + b_r).
The candidate state in GRU is computed as h'_t = tanh(W_{xh'} x_t + W_{hh'} (r_t ⊙ h_{t-1})).
The new hidden state in GRU is h_t = (1 - u_t) ⊙ h'_t + u_t ⊙ h_{t-1}.
In GRU, erasing and writing are combined into a single convex combination driven by the update gate u_t.
The reset gate r_t determines which parts of the old memory feed into the candidate state h'_t.
GRU uses 6 weight matrices.
GRU is substantially cheaper than an LSTM.
For a fixed computational budget, GRU allows more units than LSTM.
In 2015–2016, GRUs were widely adopted in NLP.
The simple summing benchmark is solved faster by a GRU than by an LSTM.
The field later reverted to using LSTMs, e.g., AlphaStar uses LSTM.
Why the LSTM remains empirically superior on hard, large-scale tasks is not fully understood.
The superiority of LSTM illustrates that neural architecture search has not found a recurrent cell that genuinely outscores the 25-year-old LSTM across a wide range of problems.
Greff et al. (2015) showed that some drastically simplified LSTM variants perform nearly as well as the LSTM.
None of the simplified variants displace the LSTM as the default robust choice.
Attention is, in large part, an interaction with working memory (Knudsen, 2007).
In human vision, the fovea is tiny.
We only see a small, sharp snippet at any instant.
The eyes move in rapid saccades, sequentially fixating on different parts of the scene.
The brain stitches together a composite picture from these fixations.
This process can be both conscious and unconscious.
The Invisible Gorilla experiment (Simons & Chabris, 1999) is a dramatic demonstration.
In the Invisible Gorilla experiment, observers concentrating on counting basketball passes completely missed a person in a gorilla suit walking through the frame.
Even when looking directly at something, you may not process it if your attention is elsewhere.
Alexander Luria emphasised the triad of attention, memory, and cognition.
Working memory acts as a very short-term buffer.
Attention acts as a filter that selects which items are passed on for deeper processing.
Selective, limited-bandwidth processing inspired early attempts to model attention in neural networks.
A neural network might also benefit from deciding what to look at.
The original motivation for attention in neural networks was efficiency, not primarily biological plausibility.
For a large image, processing the whole thing is expensive.
You can instead take a few small glimpses, using only the pixels from those parts and ignoring or blurring the rest.
This drastically reduces the input size and thus the number of parameters and computations.
Early work by Larochelle & Hinton (2010) modelled saccades as a sequence of glimpses, learning where to look next.
The idea was fully realised in "Recurrent Models of Visual Attention" (Mnih et al., 2014).
In this model, at each step a recurrent network receives a glimpse g_t derived from the current observation and previous location.
The network updates its hidden state h_t and outputs a new location l_t and action a_t.
The glimpse is computed as g_t = f_g(x_t, l_{t-1}; θ_g).
The hidden state update is h_t = f_h(h_{t-1}, g_t; θ_h).
The location is sampled from l_t ∼ p(⋅ | f_l(h_t; θ_l)).
The action is sampled from a_t ∼ p(⋅ | f_a(h_t; θ_a)).
A reward r_t is received after the action.
The objective is correct final classification.
This defines a stochastic policy π((l_t,a_t) | s_{1:t}; θ) implemented by an RNN.
The goal is to maximise expected total reward J(θ) = E[\sum_{t=1}^T r_t].
Because the choice of location is non-differentiable, reinforcement learning (REINFORCE) is used.
Subsequent work extended this to deep variational models (Ba et al., 2015) and image generation with DRAW (Gregor et al., 2015).
Recurrent visual attention is now largely outdated.
It introduced the key idea of using a recurrent mechanism to choose where to look, which later became central in encoder-decoder architectures.
Machine translation is the canonical sequence-to-sequence problem.
A recurrent language model factors a sequence X as p(X) = p(x_1) p(x_2 | x_1) … p(x_T | x_{<T}).
In an encoder-decoder for translation, an encoder RNN compresses the source sentence into a single fixed-size vector z.
A decoder RNN generates the target sentence conditioned on z (Sutskever et al., 2014; Cho et al., 2014).
The critical limitation is the bottleneck: everything must be squeezed through one vector.
Plotting translation quality against source sentence length reveals a sharp drop after short sentences.
Performance is excellent for short sentences, then drops catastrophically.
The cause is that a vector of manageable size cannot hold all the necessary information for long sentences.
Making the vector larger explodes the number of weights, making training infeasible.
The solution is to let the decoder attend to all encoder hidden states, weighted by relevance, instead of relying on a single summary vector.
The encoder still processes the input (bidirectionally) and produces a sequence of representations h_1, …, h_n, one per source token.
At each decoding step t, an attention network computes a score e_{tj} = a(z_{t-1}, h_j).
The attention weights are α_{tj} = softmax(e_{tj}).
The context vector is c_t = Σ_j α_{tj} h_j.
The context vector c_t is a convex combination of all encoder outputs.
The context vector c_t is fed to the decoder: z_t = f(s_{t-1}, y_{t-1}, c_t).
The network is never given explicit word-alignment labels.
Attention weights are learned purely from the translation loss.
They reliably discover which source tokens correspond to which target tokens (e.g., "world" → "mir").
The attention mechanism accounts for about 2% of the total parameters but is what separates usable translation from the cliff.
Visualising α matrices yields interpretable patterns: mostly diagonal for similar word order, off-diagonal for syntactic differences, reverse diagonals for reversal tasks.
Wu et al. (2016) scaled the encoder-decoder with attention to 8 encoder and 8 decoder layers of LSTMs.
They added residual connections to make training deeper layers feasible.
The bottom encoder layer was bidirectional.
This system powered Google Translate for several years.
Around 2015–2016, it produced a phase transition: post-editing machine translation became faster than translating from scratch.
The architecture can be used across modalities, e.g., CNN encoder + LSTM decoder for image captioning.
"Show and Tell" (Vinyals et al., 2015) simply fed a fixed image feature vector to an LSTM decoder.
"Show, Attend, and Tell" (Xu et al., 2015) introduced spatial attention over CNN feature vectors.
The CNN is stopped early, retaining a 14×14 grid of vectors a_i that preserve spatial layout.
At each decoding step a context vector is formed as a weighted sum φ({a_i},{α_{t,i}}) = Σ_i α_{t,i} a_i.
Two attention variants were studied: soft attention and hard attention.
Soft attention is a deterministic, differentiable convex combination, trained end-to-end.
Hard attention is stochastic sampling from the attention distribution, trained by maximising a variational lower bound.
The variational lower bound is L_s = Σ_s p(s | a) log p(y | s, a) ≤ log p(y | a).
The gradient of hard attention is ∂L_s/∂W = Σ_s p(s | a)[ ∂log p(y | s, a)/∂W + log p(y | s, a) ∂log p(s | a)/∂W ].
Hard attention is approximated by sampling \(s\) from the attention distribution \(\alpha_i\).
Attention maps are interpretable.

For the caption “a woman is throwing a frisbee in the park,” the model focuses on people for “woman,” on the throwing motion for “throwing,” on the disc for “frisbee,” and on the background for “park.”
Visual debugging using attention maps helps diagnose failures directly from the attention.
The Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) stands as arguably the single most important architecture in modern deep learning.
The original Transformer paper was presented as a more efficient way to do sequence-to-sequence modeling.
The Transformer proved to be remarkably general, effectively discovering internal correlations in sequences of vectors regardless of their origin (text, images, etc.).
The Transformer proved to be highly scalable, with performance continuing to improve as parameters and data increase from millions to trillions of parameters, without saturating.
LSTMs never achieved such scalability; they either became untrainable or saturated much earlier.
The Transformer abandons recurrence entirely and processes all tokens in parallel.
The Transformer encoder consists of a stack of identical layers.
Each encoder layer contains a multi-head self-attention sublayer followed by a position-wise feedforward network.
Residual connections and layer normalization surround each sublayer in the encoder.
The Transformer decoder follows the same pattern as the encoder but adds masked self-attention and encoder-decoder attention.
Input tokens are first converted to dense vectors by a learnable embedding layer.
Positional encodings are added to the input embeddings to inject sequence order.
The decoder is autoregressive: it generates output tokens one by one.
The decoder conditions on both its own previously generated tokens and the final encoder representations.
The decoder uses a linear + softmax head to produce next-token probabilities.
Self-attention is directly inspired by neural information retrieval.
In neural information retrieval, queries and documents are embedded into a common latent space so that relevant pairs have high dot-product similarity.
Self-attention treats every position in a set of vectors as both a query and a document.

Given an input sequence \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times L}\), the model computes queries \(Q = W_Q X\), keys \(K = W_K X\), and values \(V = W_V X\), with weight matrices \(W_Q, W_K \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times D}\) and \(W_V \in \mathbb{R}^{d_v \times D}\) (typically \(d_v = d\)).
The attention function is \(\operatorname{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{d}} Q K^{\top} \right) V\).
The matrix \(QK^\top\) contains the dot-product similarities between every query–key pair.
Scaling by \(1/\sqrt{d}\) is critical: if query and key entries behave like i.i.d. variables with zero mean and unit variance, a dot product’s expected magnitude is on the order of \(\sqrt{d}\).
Without scaling by \(1/\sqrt{d}\), the large values push the softmax into a nearly one‑hot regime (extreme saturation).
Dividing by \(\sqrt{d}\) keeps the logits at a moderate scale and the softmax smooth, enabling stable gradient flow.
In the Transformer, every position attends to every other position in a single operation.
In a recurrent network, information must travel step‑by‑step; in the Transformer a token can directly draw on any other token, regardless of distance.
The Transformer eliminates the sequential bottleneck but brings quadratic complexity in the sequence length \(L\) because the attention matrix is \(L \times L\).
Handling very long contexts (millions of tokens) requires specialized tricks to keep computation feasible.
A single attention head captures one type of relationship.
Multi‑head attention uses \(H\) independent heads, each with its own weight matrices \(W_Q^{(i)}, W_K^{(i)}, W_V^{(i)}\), producing outputs \(Z^1,\dots,Z^H\) of size \(d_v \times L\).

The head outputs are concatenated into a \((H d_v) \times L\) matrix and linearly projected back to the model dimension \(D\) via \(Z = \bigl(Z_{\text{concat}} W_O\bigr)^{\top}\) with \(W_O \in \mathbb{R}^{H d_v \times D}\).
The design separates the dimension of each head (\(d_v\)) from the model dimension \(D\), keeping the total number of parameters manageable.
If each head’s value dimension were as large as \(D\), the concatenated representation would be infeasibly large.
The multi‑head architecture gives the model a richer expressive capacity while staying practical.
Because the decoder generates tokens autoregressively, it must not see future positions.
Masked self‑attention achieves this during training: for every position \(t\), attention weights towards positions \(\ge t\) are set to \(-\infty\) before the softmax, forcing them to zero.
Masked self‑attention allows training the decoder on the whole target sequence in one forward pass while preserving causality.
Encoder‑decoder attention uses the decoder’s queries (from the partially generated output) but takes keys and values from the final encoder output.
The mechanism of encoder‑decoder attention is structurally identical to self-attention: the decoder queries retrieve information from the encoder’s representations.

The dimensions of queries and keys/values in encoder‑decoder attention need not match—the number of keys equals the encoder sequence length, while the number of queries equals the decoder prefix length.
Transformers work with subword tokens.
Using whole words leads to an unmanageably large vocabulary; using characters would make sequences far too long.
Byte‑Pair Encoding (BPE) is a data‑compression algorithm that builds a vocabulary by iteratively merging the most frequent pair of consecutive symbols.
BPE repeatedly counts adjacent pairs of tokens in the corpus, merges the most frequent pair into a new token, and replaces every occurrence of that pair with the new token.

For example, given words {cat:10, pet:12, mat:5, rat:8, eats:4}, splitting into characters yields the pair “at” with 27 occurrences; merging “at” into a new symbol \(Z\) produces {cZ:10, pet:12, mZ:5, rZ:8, eZs:4}.
The BPE merging process continues until the desired vocabulary size is reached.
In language, early BPE merges capture common morphemes like “‑ed” and “‑tion”; very common words become single tokens, while rare words are split into subword pieces.
BPE is unrelated to gradient‑based learning; it is pure data compression that yields highly efficient tokenization.
Self‑attention is completely invariant to token order—it treats the sequence as a set.
To inject position information, the Transformer adds positional encodings to the input embeddings.
The original Transformer used sinusoidal positional encodings: \(PE_{(pos, 2i)} = \sin(pos/10000^{2i/d})\), \(PE_{(pos, 2i+1)} = \cos(pos/10000^{2i/d})\).
This design ensures that the dot product of two sinusoidal positional encodings depends only on the offset \(pos_1 - pos_2\), enabling the model to easily recover relative distances.
Rotary Positional Encoding (RoPE) is a more recent and widely adopted alternative.
RoPE breaks each token vector into pairs of coordinates and rotates each pair by an angle that is a multiple of the position index and a base frequency.

In RoPE, if the pair \((x_{2i}, x_{2i+1})\) is rotated by \(\begin{pmatrix} \cos(k\theta) & -\sin(k\theta) \\ \sin(k\theta) & \cos(k\theta) \end{pmatrix}\), then rotating by \(k\theta\) and later by \(l\theta\) yields rotation by \((k+l)\theta\), giving a clean algebraic property and smooth, distance‑dependent similarity.
RoPE is now the default positional encoding in most large language models.
The Transformer trains roughly 100× faster than comparable recurrent models and achieves superior translation quality.
Because any token can directly attend to any other, long‑range dependencies are handled much better in Transformers than in RNNs.
The attention weights themselves provide a window into what the model learns—one can visualise which tokens are attended to at each layer, revealing syntactic and semantic patterns.
The Transformer’s scalability and generality have made it the foundation of virtually all subsequent advances in language and multimodal modeling.
